label: Problem set 1
title: Problem set 1: Waves and photons
summary: Practice the two pictures of light from Lesson 1: the wave equation c = λf, the photon energy E = hf = hc/λ, and reasoning about why a beam can look continuous while arriving as photons.

intro.text: This set drills the two central equations of Lesson 1, c = λf and E = hf = hc/λ, and the reasoning that goes with them. Work each one in the same order: write the equation, put in the numbers with units, then check whether the answer makes sense.
The trick with these questions is to move confidently between wavelength, frequency and photon energy. Because c is fixed, knowing any one of wavelength, frequency or energy fixes the other two.

sections.title: Working with the wave and photon equations
sections.summary: Use c = λf and E = hf = hc/λ to move between wavelength, frequency and photon energy.
keyPoints: c = λf links speed, wavelength and frequency.
E = hf, or E = hc/λ, gives the energy of one photon.
Convert wavelengths from nm to m before using them (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m).
For a quick estimate, use E(eV) ≈ 1240 / λ(nm).

blocks.text: Start from the two equations. The wave equation tells you that wavelength and frequency are locked together by the fixed speed of light; the photon equation turns either of them into an energy. A useful habit is to convert every length into metres first.
One handy shortcut: because hc = 1.99 × 10⁻²⁵ J m, a photon's energy in electronvolts is about 1240 divided by the wavelength in nanometres. That makes colour-by-colour estimates quick.

blocks.title: The wavelength and photon energy of a radio wave
blocks.given: A radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz, that is 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz. Find the wavelength and the energy of one photon. Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
steps: Wavelength from c = λf: λ = c / f = (3.0 × 10⁸) / (1.0 × 10⁸) = 3.0 m.
blocks.result: The wave is 3.0 m long and each photon carries about 6.6 × 10⁻²⁶ J.

blocks.title: Check the ballpark
blocks.body: A radio photon carries far less energy than a photon of visible light, which is why radio waves pass through your body without doing any chemical damage.

questions.question: Two lamps give light of exactly the same colour. One is brighter than the other. The brighter lamp emits:
questions.explanation: Same colour means the same frequency and so the same photon energy. "Brighter" means more photons arriving per second, that is greater intensity.

questions.question: In a vacuum, all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed whatever their wavelength.
questions.explanation: The speed in a vacuum is c for every wavelength. Wavelength and frequency change from one region of the spectrum to another, but their product, the speed, does not.

questions.question: A photon has frequency 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find its energy, in joules. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
Find the wavelength, in metres, of a wave of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
questions.explanation: λ = c / f = (3.0 × 10⁸) / (5.0 × 10¹⁴) = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m, which is 600 nm, an orange-red light.

questions.question: Which of the following has the greatest photon energy?
questions.explanation: Photon energy comes from frequency. Green light has a higher frequency than red light, infrared or radio waves, so its photons carry the most energy of these four.

questions.question: Gamma rays have longer wavelengths than visible light.
questions.explanation: Gamma rays lie at the short-wavelength end of the spectrum, shorter even than X-rays. Visible light has wavelengths hundreds of thousands of times longer.

questions.question: Which of these correctly describe electromagnetic radiation? Select all that apply.
options: it can travel through a vacuum
its energy is carried in photons
questions.explanation: It needs no medium (so it crosses empty space), it is transverse, and its energy comes in photons. It does not need air, which is why sunlight reaches us through space.

questions.question: An X-ray photon has a wavelength of 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Find its energy, in joules. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
questions.explanation: E = hc / λ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸) / 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 1.99 × 10⁻¹⁵ J, enormously more energetic than a visible photon.

questions.question: Why can microwaves travel from a satellite to your dish through empty space?
options: they need no medium, because they are oscillating fields
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic radiation is a disturbance of the electric and magnetic fields, not of matter, so it crosses a vacuum perfectly well. Sound, by contrast, would have nothing to travel through.

questions.question: Doubling the frequency of light doubles the energy of each photon.
questions.explanation: E = hf, so photon energy is proportional to frequency. Doubling f doubles E. Note that the wavelength is halved at the same time.

questions.question: Find the frequency, in hertz, of radiation of wavelength 3.0 m. Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
questions.explanation: f = c / λ = (3.0 × 10⁸) / 3.0 = 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz, a typical FM radio frequency.

questions.question: The relationship between speed, wavelength and frequency for electromagnetic waves is:
questions.explanation: For any wave, speed = wavelength × frequency, so c = λf. Rearranged, λ = c/f and f = c/λ.

questions.question: The energy of a photon is given by:
questions.explanation: A photon carries an energy proportional to its frequency through the Planck constant: E = hf.

questions.question: A photon has a frequency of 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find its energy in joules. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
Doubling the frequency of light doubles the energy of each of its photons.
questions.explanation: Since E = hf, doubling f doubles the photon energy.
